personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Dumbledore is portrayed with a carefully layered personality: warm, gently humorous, and disarming in public settings (the feast speech with its self-deprecating joke about facial hair and kiwi cups; the Christmas cracker scene with Snape; his amused 'Indeed? Er — stranger than usual, you mean?' about Trelawney), but also capable of sharp authority, cold resolve, and quiet gravitas when required. His voice is notably calm under pressure — he silences Snape with quiet finality ('I do not believe a single person inside this castle would have helped Black enter it'), handles crises with measured composure (the Fat Lady scene, the hospital wing confrontations), and deploys a particular kind of restrained playfulness that coexists with genuine moral seriousness. He never shouts. His speech patterns are deliberate, unhurried, and tend toward philosophical observation even in urgent moments (the Pettigrew life-debt speech; 'You think the dead we loved ever truly leave us?'). A key trait is his habit of indirect guidance: he gives Harry just enough — the Time-Turner hint, the window location, the 'three turns should do it' — without spelling things out, trusting Harry to reason through it. He also has a marked resistance to institutional authority (cold refusal to allow dementors inside the castle; thinly veiled contempt for Fudge) combined with genuine political limitations he acknowledges honestly. His emotional register is carefully controlled: warmth and melancholy coexist, but neither tips into sentimentality or coldness.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves most of Dumbledore's core vocal and behavioral traits. The feast speech retains his self-deprecating humor ('somewhat treacherous for those of us with facial hair'), his warm introductions of Lupin and Hagrid, and the tonal shift to gravity when announcing the dementors. His calm authority under pressure is present: the Fat Lady scene ('Secure the castle, Mr. Filch'), the Great Hall night scene with Snape (refusing to take the bait, measured dismissal of Snape's insinuation), and the hospital wing Time-Turner scene. His indirect guidance is preserved almost verbatim ('Three turns should do it... if you succeed, more than one innocent life may be spared tonight'). The twinkle, the restrained amusement ('How extraordinary!'; 'Did what?' at the door), and the philosophical register ('Mysterious thing, time. Powerful. And, when meddled with... dangerous') are all present. His cold firmness with Fudge about the dementors is present in both versions. The added film line — 'A child's voice, however honest and true, is meaningless to those who have forgotten how to listen' — is a slight stylistic addition, slightly more aphoristic than his book voice but consistent with his register.
personality_voice.difference: The film captures the main traits well. The primary loss is the depth of his emotional register in private moments: the book includes scenes where Dumbledore engages Harry in extended, philosophically rich conversations (the Patronus/James speech; the Pettigrew life-debt reflection; the gentle reassurance after the time-travel events). The film hospital wing scene compresses or omits much of this. His capacity for quiet moral complexity — telling Harry that Pettigrew's life being spared will matter, that James would have done the same, connecting the Patronus to Harry's father — is absent from the film corpus entirely. The film also omits his quietly critical stance toward Snape ('He's not unbalanced... he's just suffered a severe disappointment') which is a small but characterful moment. His Christmas dinner warmth and his gentle teasing of Trelawney are also absent from the film corpus provided, reducing visible facets of his voice.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality — calm authority, restrained humor, indirect wisdom, quiet firmness — is preserved with good fidelity. The penalty is for the loss of the private philosophical voice that defines his most characterful moments in the books: the extended reflections on death, on Pettigrew's life-debt, on James Potter, on the nature of the Patronus. These are not minor decorative scenes; they are the most distinctive expression of his voice. The film Dumbledore is recognizably himself but slightly thinner in the texture of his private register.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Dumbledore's narrative role in PoA is structural and active across multiple functions: (1) institutional protector — his refusal to allow dementors inside the castle is a persistent narrative fact that shapes the threat landscape; (2) key information holder and backstory anchor — he advised the Fidelius Charm, knew about the traitor, offered to be Secret-Keeper himself, gave orders to Hagrid the night of the Potters' deaths; (3) crisis manager — he directs the Fat Lady search, organizes the castle lockdown, conducts the night search, and manages the aftermath of Black's entry; (4) moral and plot architect — he engineers the Time-Turner solution, giving Harry and Hermione just enough to act while maintaining plausible deniability; (5) political operator — he navigates Fudge, protects Lupin, manages the dementor situation, gets the dementors removed; (6) mentor figure — he provides Harry with moral framing after the events (the Pettigrew speech, the Patronus speech). His agency is consistently active: he initiates actions, directs others, shapes outcomes.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves roles (1), (3), and (4) well. The castle lockdown and Fat Lady scene show him directing action. His role as Time-Turner architect is fully present and well-executed. His political navigation with Fudge (dementors removed, covering for Lupin) is present though compressed. Role (2) — as backstory anchor — is entirely absent from the film corpus: the Hogsmeade pub scene where Fudge and McGonagall reconstruct the Potters' history, Dumbledore's role in advising the Fidelius Charm and offering to be Secret-Keeper, and Hagrid's account of Dumbledore's orders the night of the deaths — none of this appears in the film corpus. Role (6) — the mentor function — is largely removed: the post-time-travel conversation where Dumbledore frames Harry's moral choices (Pettigrew, the Patronus, James) does not appear in the film.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The film loses Dumbledore's role as backstory anchor and post-crisis moral mentor. These are not peripheral: the backstory information establishes his deep involvement in the war against Voldemort and his relationship with the Potter family. The mentor conversation establishes his function as the person who gives Harry a moral framework for what he has done. The film replaces the mentor conversation with a brief, effective Time-Turner scene but does not restore the reflective post-crisis dialogue.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The agency loss is real but not severe: the core crisis-management and plot-architecture functions are preserved. The backstory anchor function is lost but this is partly a consequence of the film's handling of the Hogsmeade pub scene rather than a direct reassignment of Dumbledore's agency to another character. The mentor function loss is more significant — the post-crisis moral framing dialogue is omitted without reassignment to another character, simply removed. This reduces his narrative role in the final act of the story.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for what is present; reasonably inferred for what is absent based on book corpus vs. film corpus comparison

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Dumbledore's motivations in PoA are multi-layered: he is motivated by protection of Harry and the students (his resistance to the dementors is framed explicitly as protective); by loyalty to individuals he trusts against institutional pressure (his defense of Lupin, his protection of Hagrid, his trust in Sirius's innocence despite having given Ministry evidence against him); by a deep commitment to justice over law (he believes Harry and Hermione, acknowledges he cannot override Fudge, then engineers a solution that achieves justice outside official channels); and by a long view of consequence (the Pettigrew life-debt speech reveals he sees beyond immediate outcomes). His internal tension is subtle but present: he acknowledged Sirius as Secret-Keeper to the Ministry — a fact that cost him — and he cannot override the Minister even when he knows the truth, a genuine constraint that he acknowledges honestly rather than conceals.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the protection motivation and the justice-over-law motivation, most clearly in the hospital wing scene where he tells Harry and Hermione he believes them but cannot act officially, then engineers the Time-Turner solution. His loyalty to Lupin is referenced (Lupin says Dumbledore 'has already risked enough on my behalf'). His commitment to institutional boundaries is present. However, the nuance of his motivation regarding the Pettigrew life-debt — his long-view reasoning, his belief in the magic of life-debts, his quiet confidence that sparing Pettigrew was right — is entirely absent from the film.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The film simplifies his motivations to protection and procedural justice. The deeper motivation — his view of magical consequence, the life-debt reasoning, his gentle insistence that Harry's mercy was the correct moral choice even given the risk — is lost. His tension about having given evidence against Sirius is also absent. These are not the dominant motivations, but they are the ones that give him philosophical depth rather than just institutional wisdom.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The main motivations are present and functional. The simplification is real but the remaining material is correct, not wrong. The penalty reflects the loss of the philosophical layer that distinguishes him from a merely competent institutional protector.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for what is present; reasonably inferred for absences

character_arc.book_baseline: Dumbledore in PoA has a largely flat arc — he is not a character who transforms within this book. His starting position (trusted, protective, politically constrained, quietly opposed to the dementors) is his ending position. What changes is not his character but his situation: he successfully engineers an outcome that achieves justice outside official channels, gets the dementors removed, and ends the year having protected Harry and given him a moral framework for what occurred. The arc is intentionally flat, with the narrative function being to demonstrate both his power and his genuine limitations.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film preserves the flat arc accurately. Dumbledore begins and ends in the same moral and characterological position. The Time-Turner sequence, his management of the aftermath, and his departure of Lupin all track the book's trajectory. The film does not invent a new arc or falsify the existing one.
character_arc.difference: The main loss is that the ending of his arc in the books — the post-crisis mentor conversation with Harry — is absent in the film. In the books, this conversation is the culmination of his function as moral guide: he gives Harry a framework for understanding what he has done and why it was right. The film ends his involvement with the successful Time-Turner resolution and a brief 'Well?' at the door. This truncates the arc's resolution without falsifying it.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is flat in both versions, which is correct. The penalty is for the truncation of the arc's resolution: the absence of the post-crisis conversation means his function as moral guide — the thing that completes his narrative purpose for this book — is only partially delivered. The arc is compressed at its resolution, not inverted or falsified.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Dumbledore's key relationships in PoA are: (1) Harry — mentor/student with deep personal warmth, a connection rooted in Dumbledore's relationship with James; Dumbledore is the person who gives Harry moral grounding; (2) Snape — a relationship of mutual usefulness and tension; Dumbledore trusts Snape against Snape's own expressed resentments, defends him in public ('He's not unbalanced'), and manages his jealousy with quiet authority; (3) Lupin — a relationship of long-standing loyalty; Dumbledore gave Lupin his place at Hogwarts as both child and adult, an act of profound trust that Lupin explicitly describes as defining his life; (4) Fudge — a political relationship of constrained authority, where Dumbledore must operate within Fudge's nominal power while quietly outmaneuvering him.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Dumbledore-Snape dynamic is preserved with good fidelity: the cold dismissal in the Great Hall ('I do not believe a single professor...'), the quiet management in the hospital wing ('That will do, Severus'), and the 'He's not unbalanced' line — all present in the book corpus but the last is absent from the film corpus. The Dumbledore-Lupin relationship is referenced but not dramatized: Lupin says Dumbledore has 'already risked enough' on his behalf, and Dumbledore sees him off at his office door, but the weight of that relationship — Dumbledore's decades of loyalty and the trust Lupin almost betrayed — is not developed. The Dumbledore-Harry mentor relationship is the most significantly reduced: the post-crisis conversation that defines this relationship's emotional texture in PoA is absent. The Dumbledore-Fudge political dynamic is present and functional.
key_relationships.difference: The Dumbledore-Harry relationship loses its most defining scene in this book. The Dumbledore-Lupin relationship is gestured at but not developed. The Dumbledore-Snape dynamic is mostly present. The Dumbledore-Fudge dynamic is intact.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The loss of the post-crisis Harry conversation is the most significant relationship penalty: it is the moment where the emotional dynamic of this relationship is most clearly expressed. The Lupin relationship is compressed but its key beat (the farewell, the acknowledgment of debt) is present. The Snape dynamic loses one characteristic line but is otherwise intact.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Dumbledore's complexity in PoA comes from several sources: (1) the coexistence of genuine limitation and great power — he cannot override Fudge, he cannot prevent Pettigrew's escape, he cannot stop the dementor attack, yet he is the most powerful figure in the narrative; (2) his long-view moral philosophy, expressed most fully in the Pettigrew life-debt speech, which reveals him as someone who thinks in terms of magical consequence and human debt rather than immediate justice; (3) his gentle but precise management of others' emotions — with Snape, with Fudge, with Harry — which is always purposeful rather than merely diplomatic; (4) the backstory material that reveals he suspected betrayal before the Potters died and offered himself as Secret-Keeper, a detail that gives him moral weight and genuine vulnerability; (5) his quiet playfulness — the Christmas cracker scene, the Trelawney teasing — that humanizes him without undermining his authority.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves (1) and (3) adequately. The limitation/power tension is present in the hospital wing scene. His management of Snape and Fudge is mostly intact. (2) is entirely absent — the life-debt speech and the moral philosophy of consequence are not in the film. (4) is entirely absent — the backstory material about Dumbledore's role in the Fidelius Charm is not in the film corpus. (5) is partially present — the feast humor is there but the Christmas cracker scene and the Trelawney teasing are absent.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film loses the philosophical layer of Dumbledore's character, the backstory depth that gives him moral weight, and a significant portion of his humanizing humor. What remains is a competent, warm, authoritative headmaster. What is missing is the person whose long view of history, whose deep personal connection to the Potters, and whose moral philosophy give him the specific texture that distinguishes book-Dumbledore from a generic wise mentor.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: This is the dimension where the adaptation's compression does the most cumulative damage. No single element that is lost is catastrophic, but together they remove the material that makes Dumbledore more than a plot-functional wise figure. The life-debt speech, the backstory revelations, and the post-crisis mentor conversation are not redundant material — they are the material that gives him philosophical and emotional depth.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for what is present; directly evidenced (by absence) for what is missing

lost_or_transferred_material: The post-crisis mentor conversation with Harry (Pettigrew life-debt speech; 'You think the dead we loved ever truly leave us?'; Patronus/James reflection) — omitted entirely from the film
Dumbledore's backstory role in advising the Fidelius Charm and offering to be Secret-Keeper himself — present in book Hogsmeade pub scene, absent from film
Hagrid's account of Dumbledore's orders the night of the Potters' deaths — present in book, absent from film corpus
The 'He's not unbalanced... he's just suffered a severe disappointment' exchange with Fudge about Snape — present in books, absent from film corpus
The Christmas dinner scene — Dumbledore's warmth, humor with Trelawney, management of Snape — absent from film corpus
Dumbledore's explicit acknowledgment that he gave Ministry evidence that Sirius was Secret-Keeper — present in book hospital wing scene, absent from film
The moral framing of Harry's choice to spare Pettigrew ('It does not... you did a very noble thing') — absent from film
score_caps_applied: Cap 1 applied (no higher than 85): the film removes a major portion of Dumbledore's complexity, specifically his philosophical register, backstory depth, and post-crisis mentor function, even though the remaining material is superficially faithful. Score kept below 85.
Cap 2 not triggered: key relationships are altered but not substantially changed — the Dumbledore-Harry relationship is compressed rather than falsified.
Cap 3 not triggered: no core book function or emotional beat is transferred to another character; they are omitted rather than reassigned.
key_observations: The film's Dumbledore is recognizably and largely faithfully rendered in his surface traits — calm authority, restrained humor, indirect wisdom, and political firmness — and his structural roles as crisis manager and Time-Turner architect are well preserved. The adaptation's significant cost is the near-total removal of his private, philosophical register: the post-crisis conversations with Harry that define his mentor function in PoA, the backstory material that gives him moral depth and personal stakes, and the life-debt reasoning that reveals his long-view moral philosophy. The film Dumbledore is correct in type but thin in texture. He functions as a wise, warm headmaster; he does not function as the philosophically complex, historically weighted figure the books establish. The total of 77 reflects a portrayal that is substantially faithful in visible traits and structural role but meaningfully reduced in the dimensions that make the character rich.
